Author: @GamersNexus
Content:
This event was super fun! Not everything in here is because of Windows 10 support ending; Kramden does this all the time, for any computer or reason. That's also why you see some Macs in here. Some more background if you're curious: Kramden gets a mix of e-waste and donated / retired machines from local individuals and from companies. Sometimes, these have perfectly good hardware, sometimes they have one or two broken things. They then work with volunteers (like in this episode) to reclaim anything valuable that could be used for education or cobbled-together into a new machine. A good example is the 12700K: This was in there because some company or person got rid of the computer, but obviously that's still a great part. The next step is to identify whatever was broken in the system, save the good parts, and repurpose them (or sell them to fund the classroom program). Anything unusable, such as just broken hardware or obsolete hardware, is broken down into recyclables and trash, sorted, and sent to the right groups to smelt down or dispose of. They are awesome.
Find Kramden here! https://kramden.org/ (they do local sales also of donated items, sometimes including things we drop off! They also do classes and training on how to use computers, including Ubuntu)
Find Canonical and Ubuntu here: https://ubuntu.com/
Check out our video with Wendell talking about future Linux benchmarking plans: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5O6tQYJSEMw
Buy our Honey Pot charity T-shirt! Profits get split between Kramden, Archive.org, and PIRG: https://store.gamersnexus.net/products/honey-pot-foil-tshirt-100pct-cotton-limited
Watch our RAM installation competition at Kramden previously: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9x8FeaX71tg

Author: @xyphur
Content:
Linux is fine and dandy for all the things it is good at, but a daily desktop OS is not one of those things. Firefox on Linux still doesn't even have hardware video acceleration out of the box, and it's a bloody faff to get it working. On Nvidia, it requires a translation layer between VA-API and NVDEC. In other works: a hack. And that sums up my experience with trying to use various Linux distros as a desktop OS. Every time I try, there's at least a handful of things that I need to dive into the terminal to get working, and out of them, there's always a few that just don't, or require a ridiculous hack be done that breaks other things. You shouldn't have to recompile a kernel on a desktop OS to gain functionality that has been baked into Windows for a decade or more. A desktop OS should Just Work(tm). A desktop OS should be able to be configured completely using the GUI, so everyone and their grandmother can use it. Grandma isn't about to fire up a terminal and start editing files, patching things, recompiling the kernel, etc etc. It's asinine to think that is acceptable.

You'd be better off installing Win 10 IoT Enterprise LTSC on these machines. You get a mature OS that has wide compatibility, functionality, and will continue receiving updates until 2032. Maybe at that point, when LTSC support dries up, Linux might be ready for prime-time daily driver use, but it honestly just isn't yet - despite my wishes and repeated attempts to the contrary. I want to like it.

Author: @Mvvkt
Content: I hate being an "actually" guy but Windows 11 is actually "supported" unofficially all the way down until AMD FX (AMD Bulldozer) and Intel Sandy Bridge (i3/5/7 2xxx) line of CPUs. It requires SSE 4.2 and POPCNT instruction sets. So 10-13 year old computers could potentially still run Windows 11. So anybody with an "old" CPU/Computer do consider installing Windows 11 if you're not quite ready for Linux yet. Run CPU Z, check the supported instruction sets, if you're good to go, great! Otherwise you're SOL and need to move on to GNU/Linux.

Content:
the Radeon PRO WX3100 is about the performance of a GTX 470 but with 4GB GDDR5 RAM instead of just 1GB. Its a low power Workstation GPU with limited output capability. this GPU is faster in some scenarios as the GTX 470 but uses way less power, i think in the range of 30W to 75W. Yeah in know modern GPUs have more but back then this GPU was worth 1000€ and more the GTX 470 was cheap even for the same performance. The key difference here is, the GTX is a live Render optimized GPU the Radeon Pro WX3100 is a Task based Render optimized GPU its over all Die is different. this GPU doesnt know what Vsync is and has no idea of DirectX and other bullshit. I mean yeah it knows what what DirectX is but it does only support the minimum requirements to work it cant do fancy stuff. its purely designt to do Task-based Rendering. Author: @flybywire5866
Content:
My actual PC was built by me in november 2019. I9-9900k, 2080TI, all watercooled. It still works just fine for all the games I want to play, and I was able to upgrade it to Windows 11 without any problems. With all the talk about Windows, AI monitoring users, likely a subscription model and whatnot, I was getting more and more uncomfortable with Windows. What if one day MS says pay up or it wont boot anymore? I assume they have the technical means to do so, and the current US government would cheer them on. I don't want to sleepwalk into it, so something had to be done.
I realized my PC has a free SSD slot. At the End of July I bought another SSD and installed Ubuntu on it. So far it has been an adventure to get things running. It's definitely not as polished as windows. However, with some perseverance it is doable. You must enter long cryptic commands, which you have to find on the internet in the first place, into the terminal to make things work. That is not suitable for everyone, and I guess this is what prevents Linux from being more popular. Getting Opera to play every video was another adventure.
However, at the end of the day it does work. The more users Linux has, the more development will be there. The more Linux compatible software will be offered.
I am done with Windows.

Author: @kooijbas
Content:
I try to to install Linux on my desktop every 5 years since the year 2000. Tried for the last time 2 weeks ago with CachyOS (previous tries were with Ubuntu and Mint). It still didn't work and is not suitable for normal users, after 25 years of trying. I downloaded the ISO, then needed a tool to make a bootable USB (which wasn't documented on the site).  Then I booted from the USB and was presented with a GUI. Mouse didn't work. Was unclear how to proceed, it looked like I was done, but this was the install program. After clicking install I needed to create a partition and select a bootloader. No descriptions of what even a bootloader is or what the differences were, so I went with the one that said default. Then created a partition of 128GB, install started and I got an error that the system partition was full. Tried it again with a 256GB partition and got the same thing with a non-descript error message. 

Now, I'm sure a ton of you will tell me the solution to this, or say skill issue, but that is not the point. A regular user that does not spend his days working with computers or has them as a hobby will not understand any of this or be able to work through this without giving up. Ubuntu is the only one I would dare to give to my parents.

Our cars will stop receiving security updates at a time chosen at the discretion of the manufacturer and its suppliers. The only feasible way to push against this is free software and hardware. Author: @jtgam2086
Content:
It is very likely that you can get another year of MS10 support for free, simply go into your settings -> Update & Security -> Windows Update. From there, check the link on the right (should be near the top) to get enrolled in Extended Security Updates. Please keep in mind that you need to be on the latest Windows Update - if you aren't then go ahead and update windows. When enrolling, you have three options:

1) You can enroll if you are syncing with OneDrive - this is free and no subscription is required.
2) You can redeem 1000 Microsoft Points if you have them to enroll immediately.
3) If you do not want or are unable enroll via one of the other methods, you can pay $30.

These options will be displayed to you upon clicking the link to enroll. if you are already syncing with OneDrive, then you can immediately enroll without doing anything further. It's worth checking at the very least if you are unsure.

Author: @blahorgaslisk7763
Content:
I've never worked on "trash pick" PC's. The worst I worked on was when a large company had a break in at their main office. It was a very well planned move. They totally defeated the burglar alarm making it likely they had an inside source. They also had brought in a huge load of people who didn't know anything about computers and just got told to grab all memory, the processor and the hard drives from all machines. So they had gone through about a hundred offices and wrecked every machine they found. It was almost funny as the machines was extremely simple to open with a single big thumb screw you removed in a couple of seconds and the case came off. But it seemed only one of the people they brought in figured this out as only a few machines was opened that way. Most had been broken open with force which must have taken a lot longer than opening them the right way. Then they had ripped the memories from the slots and did the same to the processors. That was also interesting to see as most of the machines had the processor ripped out of the ZIF socket without any care to open the lever first. There were even a few pins left in some of the sockets. 

They called me in to try to see if any of the machines could be saved or if they would have to buy all new machines. I think I was able to puzzle together something like 30 working machines out of a total of about 70. And that was with new processors, memory and HDD's. It also took about ten new cases. The rest had broken motherboards and cases that just wasn't possible to save.

I also remember a computer seller who had problems. They were a rather new company and had sold a computer they bought from Taiwan but had no technical knowledge themselves. So when they got about 30% of the machines returned as non working it was rather expensive for them having to replace these with new machines. So I worked there for a couple of days testing and combining the machines to try to save them some money. I got about half of them working but a lot of the motherboards just weren't reliable. Going with unknown brands can save you money, but if you are aren't lucky they can cost you money.

I have to say thinking of it like that I'm surprised that we had as few problems with the machines we sold at the company I worked at. Sure we had some problems with portables, but all in all it was remarkably few that was a total failure. In most cases it was HDDs or memory that failed. And for the portables we had a good supply of spare parts. But of the stationary machines that I built I don't think we had more than a 1% return under warranty. I think a lot of it was that we used good quality motherboards. Initially it was almost exclusively ASUS and AOpen. This was when ASUS was still a rather small manufacturer and really did try to provide good quality motherboards, and AOpen was, if I remember correctly a offshoot from Acer. We used both their motherboards and their cases which was an interesting design. OTher than that there were a lot of InWin cases. Processors were all Intel back then, Memory from Samsung and HDD's from Maxtor, Conner, Seagate and all the usual so no strange parts there. The multi I/O cards was the most exotic as they were imported from Taiwan and came more and more advanced over time. No brand I remember particularly but they were basically reliable every one. It was interesting to see. The first computers had a graphics card, a HDD controller, a FDD controller and a I/O card with both two serial ports and a parallell port. This we called a SerPar card. Rather soon the HDD, FDD and serial and parallell ports were integrated into one card. Then we got the Local buss slots. At first there were no standard and the different motherboard manufacturers had their own design, but pretty soon the VLB slot was standardized. That's the Vesa Local Bus slot. The other slots in the machine was still ISA standard. The VLB cards also evolved and there were some that included both graphics card and all the I/O and drive controllers in one unit. But Sound cards was still their own part. And no, sound was not integrated on the motherboards for many years to come.

And I have no idea why Iäm writhing all of this... So I better stop now...

Author: @denikec
Content:
I have installed Linux, dual booting Manjaro KDE Plasma next to Win11
Under 3 months these happened to me:
- I had to read the documentation 3 times until I could properly set up reFind
- moving windows, switching desktops, and system notifications appearing make the entire system lag on NVIDIA cards on X11
- you can not undervolt NVIDIA cards on linux without writing some python script that runs automatically, and even that just shifts the curve by a certain offset
- VR does not work properly, my headset does not have linux software, and ALVR is laggy and unusable
- My racing wheel does not have drivers, there is one someone made but it does not work properly
- Games run considerably worse on Proton (to be expected) - minecraft runs better than on windows (big plus)
- RGB did not work. I had to open a support ticket on openRGB to find out some incredibly convoluted way of getting the Chroma to work
- OpenRGB, unless killed by a script right before restart, would cause the ENTIRE COMPUTER to hang 
- Wayland does not lag on NVIDIA, however I can not make screenshots because Flameshot is broken (spectacle works tho), and Remote Desktop will NOT work with multiple monitors
- There is no ShareX alternative, if you want to record videos on desktop you will need to write an ffmpeg script from scratch. (I looked and looked, there are tools that capture video, but not sound, or capture gifs only.)
- Proton Experimental had a faulty update, and for some reason Lutris defaulted to it, which caused approximately 5000 explorer.exe processes to start up, so many that Resource manager would crash when trying to count them, crashing everything else
- Sometimes when moving widgets around the trays in KDE Plasma, the entire UI would crash if I hovered over a widget
- Moving icons on trays sometimes stopped working, requiring a full restart of the UI
- System update of 300 packages, then restarted PC and Kwin was crash looping until a fix was deployed days later

And what do I get in return?
""privacy"" and stuff is a bit faster. Sure, if my PC didn't support win11 it would be different, but not really because I'd use the workaround to install it.
Linux is not worth it for me, it was pure suffering.
>inb4 try another distro
I spent months setting this one up, and I finally got it looking how I want it to. And I died inside. 
Sure, it might be better on another distro, but I'm not trying anymore, if it works for you then great.

Content: We've been installing Linux Mint for a few years on old hardware (normally 2nd and 3rd gen ex corporate machines).  This works great if you don't want to run scanning/printing software, CAD, Adobe or the Microsoft desktop apps.  There are workarounds even for this (new printer sometimes), but in general a perfectly working machine can be made from something older for free (if you do all the work yourself) or for a bit of time from a PC company (like mine).  If you have ever used a Chromebook, then Linux has the same limitations for the "normal" Windows apps, but if you fancy running alternative software, Linux gives you a platform to expand and do nearly everything a Windows PC would do.  The fact that even perfectly great 7th generation machines can't officially run Windows 11 is a travesty.  However, have a look at enrolling these into ESU, which gets another year of Windows 10 support for free if you have a Microsoft personal account (in the UK at least).  This sometimes needs a registry edit to make the enrol button appear on Windows 10 update.

Author: @gstormcz
Content:
Linux is easy to run and simple to install. Most Office apps and tools are available or have good alternatives. It’s light, fast, and runs smoother than Windows — no stuttering.

But once the hardware interacts deeply with the OS core, things can get tricky. The ext4 filesystem makes you incompatible with Windows, and recovering data from it usually requires Linux itself.

I’m curious if Steve will ever do a games collection benchmark on Linux.

I only wanted to play a couple of DX9/DX11 games, but being forced to use Steam makes it pointless when you already have accounts outside Steam or want to join public tests. Wine isn’t easy to configure, and game developers rarely care about the 1–2% Linux market share — sadly.

I highly recommend store data on some compatible external USB/HDD drive to get backup if your experience or decision make you to Windows some day.

Author: @cryptophoenix2023
Content:
I recently discovered that my parents had quite a collection of useless PCs that were all handicapped by Windows and low-end hardware--not dead, just handicapped. Some were still running on HDDs. Every one of them was consigned to an inevitable landfill fate--my parents just hadn't gotten around to it (after all these years). I also have my old tower PC that I used for years, still running a 2nd gen i5, which I also consigned to the same fate a few years ago--I just held onto it thinking that maybe I could one day find *some* kind of use for it. I switched to Linux in February this year, and it's opened a whole new world now.

MX Linux KDE has breathed a second life into every one of them. I love that KDE Plasma has settings for touchscreen devices, as two of the laptops have touchscreens on them, so I've had a blast customizing them for with a touchscreen-centric workflow. It's a whole different way to interact with a PC I've never experienced before, and it's really cool to be able to do that with KDE Plasma.

I'm surprised at how powerful Linux is for giving old hardware a useful purpose again that isn't frustrating to use. Even when it's running on an HDD the performance is still more than doable--once you get past the 10-20 second start time for programs, at least, the rest of the OS runs nicely. 

It's a travesty that companies don't make their software and hardware for Linux, given how efficient, lightweight, and customizable it is--and the fact it's free and easy to install. Thanks to Linux, I now have more PCs than I will ever need, and I will eagerly take any PC that someone thinks is garbage.

And anyone who throws a PC or laptop in the trash will be informed that nuclear waste has a half-life, e-waste does not.

One of the fundamental problem is that we don't live in an economic system, we live in a market system. And the fact of the matter is that a market system is based on buying and selling, in which everyone seeks to maximise profit in each transaction. But it gets worse, because that constant pursuit of profit means that there must be infinite exponential growth, which is obviously not possible. It also means that in order for there to be growth, the quality of goods and services must constantly go down, while prices must constantly go up. In fact, a system that requires growth to function can never reach equilibrium. The evidence of this is openly available, all you have to do is look at product quality and price over time. Whereas economics means work applied by humans to resources to meet human needs. The very moment you attach money to any economic activity it destroys the economics of that particular activity and turns into profit seeking activity. The irony of it all, is that a market system doesn't work without economics either, but a market system will always result in the destruction of economics.

But that's a scratch of the surface kind of stuff. If you want to understand the problem at its root you have to ask a lot of questions, here's a couple:

Author: @Yamyatos
Content:
Linux is pretty alright for working on it. Using it on my office laptop for software development, even if im not one of those diehard Linux fans personally. 
As a gamer at heart, there is primarily two things holding Linux back. While the overwhelming majority of games runs well on Linux, there is the issue with anticheats requiring kernel level access, which Linux wont give them. Meaning you cant play stuff like.. say.. Helldivers. And generally much / most of the online stuff, which really will stop people from ditching Windows in favor of Linux for private use.
Secondly and equally importantly: ease of use. Linux is not rocket science, but i feel like those arguing it's super easy to use underestimate the computer illiteracy of the average user. The person i've been gaming with for like 2 decades is barely capable of converting something to a PDF and considers using AI the equivalent of magic. No, the average Linux forum post to help with issues, or even guides, is absolutely, certainly and verifiably not at a level the average user finds helpful. Heck, some of them feel like a different language to me and i have a masters degree in computer sciences. Then there is some distributions that attempt to make stuff easier by having, essentially, an app store (Xubuntu, looking at you) but causing tons of follow-up issues with that. Other distributions are great.. but behind in drivers or other necessary support by months or years, which is also a deterrent for some users. Especially gamers, if they cant play a game for months. One may argue that the hundreds of distributions themselves are also not exactly helping with people adopting Linux, since it's another layer of deterrence, having to even just get into the pros and cons of all these distributions.

But it's not all bad. Steam and Steamdeck were *huge* in terms of getting stuff working on Linux. What we are missing is really just a more easy to use, robust (semi-official) and up to date linux distribution with wide support for beginners and the anti cheat issue being addressed. Either of which being done puts pressure on the other happening faster. I cant wait to finally ditch Windows for good. I liked Windows 7.. and i grew to love Windows 10 even. But i'm done with their nonsense end of support every couple years, and them implementing wild design changes nobody asked for. That said, certain Linux distributions break just as commonly from (LTS) upgrades as Windows does.. so not like you are free of disruptions in the Linux world.

Author: @Ahand59
Content: Linux is good at running apps that are designed for it, business software, utilities, etc..., but for anyone wanting a "gaming PC", Linux will always lag behind Windows performance. Most of the top games are written for Windows. Some are ported to Linux, while others either work or mostly work, but does that mean the game on that PC will work as well as it does with Windows? No! Linux machines don't have driver updates as frequently as Windows does. That said, most motherboards don't have Linux drivers written specifically for them, by their manufacturer.  This means your motherboard will probably work, but it probably won't perform as well as games typically do with Windows. This is the crux of the Linux VS. Windows dilemma. Linux may support your game, but you'll probably notice performance issues...

Author: @notuxnobux
Content: It looks like it's not standard ubuntu which is good. Standard ubuntu is a terrible choice these days for old computers, since ubuntu now uses snaps and wayland. Snaps causes applications to startup much slower, especially on hdd disks. The startup of libre office can go from 1.5 seconds to over 10 seconds just because of snaps. Wayland doesn't also work properly (or not at all) on older gpus that are so old that they are unable to get the latest drivers. This is especially true on nvidia. A good alternative is linux mint which doesn't suffer from either of those issues.

Author: @mono_vt
Content:
Disclosure: I have some technical background, I'm not afraid to experiment and had *basic* experience with Linux. My experience may not mirror yours.

Got tired of M$'s 💩. Been on Linux for 3 and a half years, after a game I was playing at the time reportedly starting working under Proton. 

I originally tried Mint, but it couldn't find my SSD to install. I tried Solus Budgie, stayed on that for a week. Was bothered by the GTK3/4 UI differences. Tried Pop!_OS (Because I can read, IYKYK), all seems good, could install Steam, play games, stayed on that for a while, approximately 2 years. Then I got bored and moved to Solus KDE because I wanted KDE Plasma 6, since Kubuntu wasn't getting it at the time. It's been really good despite not being "mainstream"! Rather than being a bi-yearly release schedule, it has somewhat regular updates. Mind you, You, the user get to decide what and when to update.

* Anti-cheat... honestly am not as bothered as I could be? Some anti-cheat works, some don't. If a game chooses not to run, then I choose not to buy. Check Proton DB beforehand. Fair warning though, some games that run Denuvo have a daily activation limit, and each time you change Proton version adds 1 activation to that tally. It's entirely possible to be locked out of that game for the day. ⛵ 
* Actually gaming. This is one of the main reasons I moved, but it was kind of an AMD thing as well. When I moved, OpenGL was so much better on Linux and I do still play a decent amount of Minecraft. I know that after some time, AMD had improved OpenGL on Windows but it's too late for me. Add in Lutris making legacy games easier/better to play, I'm a very happy gamer indeed. Besides that I play some "WoW" and emulate oldish games, both of which I enjoy greatly. Some games may even run better under Proton, which is a nice surprise.
* Game videos. Some games use video formats that aren't well supported under Linux. Valve's Proton can often work around the issue and Proton-GE usually makes the rest work. However, a handful of game's videos remain broken. Some of those games ship with the video files unencrypted and you can re-encode them to a different format yourself and trick the game into loading them with symlinks. Of my Steam library I had just one game I had to do this with. I don't expect the average user to have to do this.
* Streaming, recording. Actually fine. I don't have a Streamdeck, but I use Easy Effects for my equaliser, and QPWGraph to route audio if needed. Just standard OBS for me. Microphone and camera works fine too.
* Discord. Ideally would move away from Discord, but I can't do this yet. I have Element and ReVolt installed, but a lot of the people I talk to still use Discord so yeah. I heard of growing pains with Wayland but I don't personally know anything about that.
* Bluetooth and Wi-fi. ALWAYS check what it is that you're actually buying. If you don't know what you're buying, then you don't know it'll work. I did my research on Wi-fi adapters (there's actually a list for this) and found one that worked first try. On the other hand, I got a Bluetooth adapter as a gift a couple years back and wasn't able to make it work. No, I don't have it any more, so I don't know if it works now or not.
* Controller. I have an 8bitdo ultimate Bluetooth, and Steam allows me to set it up just so, depending on whether I want the Switch mode for gyro or Xinput mode for analog triggers. I also have a Logitech G27 that works great. However,
* Non-mainstream hardware. If you've got something that's not mainstream or well-known, you can end up SOL. For example, HOSAS setups may confuse Linux because they have the same address, or maybe you've got the Generic Racing Wheel 42069 and there's no driver for it.
* GPU software. There is no software that does everything AMD Adrenaline Software does yet. I'd use LACT for setting up fan curves, or GPU adjustments. Anything related to game settings is usually done in-game.
* I'm an avid customisation fan, and KDE for me allows me to set it up just the way I want. Klassy style and Panel Colourizer... *chef's kiss* 
* Somehow managed to run a secondary drive for a year without a table, so couldn't make a second partition. Solution was backup drive and reformat. Time consuming but not difficult to fix. 🤷‍♂

Author: @PhilipStorry
Content:
Thank you - and Kramden - for saving these machines and recycling the rest.
As someone who's working in IT I'd like to say that whilst we want to get the maximum lifespan from our hardware, there are some practical limiting factors which explain why many of those machines were sent for recycling.
The main one is the warranty/service plan period - after that expires any repair call outs become expensive, so if a machine develops a fault then replacing and sending it for recycling it is a better option than attempting repairs.
The second point would be that the time of the IT staff has a cost, and in today's world of constant software updates and security patching it may simply not be worth their time to repair a machine - they could be doing something more valuable for the organisation. This is especially true if you don't know what the fault is, as it could easily become a time sink.
The last point is an edge case in support, but one overlooked by those not working in or with regulated industries. (Finance, healthcare, etc.) If a machine - or a component in a machine - goes out of support from its manufacturer, then you're not getting security patches for it. So it's automatically a security risk, and shouldn't be kept in use. It's potentially fine for many other use cases, but will still be sent for recycling.
There's other reasons, but those are the main ones.
Thanks again for this! ❤

Author: @bluephreakr
Content:
Hello, EndeavourOS user here. Also, a former Manjaro user. Also, a former Ubuntu user. Also, a former Debian user. in my near twenty-year "Career" of daily-driving a Linux distro (on-and-off) I'm grateful for the pportunity to try Ubuntu offered by soe dude via AIM uears ago, before AIM / Yahoo! / Oath killed their chat platforms and enjoyed open-source computing in various ways for years thereon. As a current EndeavourOS user, I can tell people this stuff is not hard to manage.

Lots of people see EndeavourOS and CachyOS as more difficult options because they're based on Arch. But I can tell you a few secrets to help make the process of managing these distros less painful. If you don't mind mixing desktop application interfaces or are using KDE Plasma / Qt5 / Qt6 already, then Octopi is a fantastic software solution to go along with KDE Discover; the latter handles "Metapackages" and flatpak, the former handles individual packages and software built with scripts delivered via the Arch User Repository; a resource of third-party applications for things not in Arch's standard repositories.

The GTK-based alternative for an all-in-one interface which hail from the kind people working on Manjaro — known as Pamac, has two graphical primary interfaces made available from third-parties publishing modified binaries for this software on the AUR; *pamac-aur* (built using GTK4 + LibAdwaita; exactly as every standard app for GNOME Shell is), and *pamac-gtk3* (buiilt using GTK3, good for older GTK-based desktops). I'll provide how in the terminal to build that without fancy tools below, explaining pauses where $EDITOR is involved as we go along (though, you can replace that with your graphical text editor of preference if using nano, [(neo)(vi[m])] or emacs isn't your speed):
———
_Replace $AUR with the domain for Arch User Repository; subtituted to prevent automated moderation from removing this post._
_Using _*_pamac-gtk3_*_ as example; _*_pamac-aur_*_ doesn't need additional user intervention to build for preference._
cd /tmp
git clone $AUR/libpamac-aur
git clone $AUR/pamac-cli
git clone $AUR/pamac-gtk3
cd ./libpamac-aur
$EDITOR ./PKGBUILD
_Set to _*_1_*_ either of the option for "Universal" packaging formats. Flatpak by itself _*_heavily_*_ recommended. You _*_must_*_ re-build this package if you intend to change available features in-future._
makepkg -si
cd ../pamac-cli
makepkg -si
cd ../pamac-gtk3
$EDITOR ./PKGBUILD
_Scroll down to where you see "options=('debug')'" (line 37 presently) and delete it to omit creation of a debug package._
makepkg -si
pamac-tray &
———
Once you open Pamac Manager, the overflow menu left of window controls hide option to access the _preferences_ dialogue. Make further changes for available features there and enjoy an easy means of updating all of your system software packages.

As observed above, it seems like _a lot_ of steps to create something, but all of the heavy work was done for you by somebody else; you're jut doing the light work of obtaining it. Practice this in a terminal and you probably wouldn't need the assists it'll provide, but as a convenience option when coming back home from work, it's _fun_ to just click a few buttons and make _the magic_ happen, whether you're too busy or too drunk to think about this computer junk all day.

However you go about making your open-source journey easier, there will always be people to help, Linux distributions are _easier-than-ever_ to use, it's just a matter of not being so hard. _We're waiting for you._

Author: @RepairWins
Content:
I run a non-profit where we repair and refurbish faulty electronics (mostly laptops) for resale or for lease to other businesses. The proceeds raised go to training young / digitally excluded / otherwise disadvantaged people how to repair electronics. We also sometimes have enough cash spare to donate devices to people who need them in our local community (Birmingham, UK)

Anyway, the amount of Windows 10 only laptops we're offered is unbelievable. We don't even have to pay for them. We're doing the businesses a favour by taking them for free. The UK is the 2nd biggest producer of e-waster per head of population as our tax laws incentivise waste generation but even so, the pile of machines that has appeared in the last 6 months is... well, it's a lot. Whilst you can get another year of support by registering for a Microsoft account, it's mostly needless waste.

Don't get me wrong, we sometimes see 15 year old Lenovo ThinkPad T410s which are no use to 90% of people but the majority of machines are only 6 or 7 years old and work perfectly for most people. We're truly lucky to have Linux. Just think of all the waste it has prevented!

Content:
It's also worth paying attention to all of the low-power machines out there on the market that had Windows installed for no reason other than HP or Dell or whoever had 50 bazillion licenses in inventory.

A little while ago I picked up an HP stream laptop as junk and after taking it apart and finding out it had half as much RAM as it could hold and there was a barrel from a power cable broken off in the jack, I yanked the broken bit and tossed in an 8gb stick of RAM I recycled out of another system that got an upgrade, and it now gets like 10 hours of battery life running Debian since it was always basically an X86 Chromebook.

4gb of ram and a soldered-on EMMC boot drive + Windows really explains why it got abandoned but it runs 4k video and everything web-related I've thrown at it with some headroom to spare. Author: @PXAbstraction
Content: This is exactly what I'm doing. I'm a senior projects guy at a local MSP and have worked out with my employer than when clients want to retire systems, we'll propose them giving them to me, on agreement that we provide proof of wiping (not destroying) the drives. If machines can't install Windows 11, I will put Linux on them (previously Linux Mint, now Zorin OS because it looks almost exactly like Windows) and then I donate the machines to a local charity that uses them for educational purposes or to assist the less fortunate. These people don't need anything specific about Windows and anything they would need a computer for can be easily accomplished in Linux. I'm a happy Windows daily driver (yes, we exist) and don't think it's unreasonable for Microsoft to stop supporting a 10 year old OS that's long past being sold, especially when they've telegraphed it years in advance, but Linux is an absolute saviour here. Over the years, I've managed to donate over 300 devices and I'm hoping I can keep doing this for years. It feels good both to help charity and also save a lot of poison from landfills. I wish we had something on the scope of the Kramden Institute where I live.

Author: @benjaminlynch9958
Content:
Great video Steve.

I’m going through the process of installing Linux (Arch) on my Surface Laptop as I type this. It’s got 4GB of Ram, 128GB of SSD, and a dual core processor. It barely boots windows 10 today, and system updates typically take 45 minutes on a good day.

A couple pointers for people like me who are dealing with obsolete hardware with limited upgrade options: go with a version of Linux that supports KDE rather than Gnome. That switch alone saved me 200MB of RAM (5% of capacity in my case). And if you’re feeling adventurous, compile a custom kernel rather than using the binary that comes as the default. It’s definitely more of an advanced option, but the default kernel has support for every piece of hardware under the sun, and that results in a lot of bloat and big memory footprint. Going in and selecting support for your specific hardware and leaving out everything you’ll never use (like FPGA’s, all IDE devices, CD-ROM support, etc) will really cut down on the size of the kernel and the amount of memory it uses. In my case, that means the system will use the SSD as a Swap file considerably less which will in turn make that SSD last a lot longer. And that’s to say nothing of the performance improvements. For those who want to compile a kernel from scratch, it’s a bit daunting the first time, but a good way to get over that hump is to set up a Virtual Machine (eg in Virtual Box) and do it a couple times there first. Once you get the hang of it, it’s not any more difficult than installing a game from Steam. And there are tons of tutorials online for how to do it.

Author: @Luckdragon2000
Content:
THANK YOU for doing a Linux episode! I played with SuSE Linux, my very first dive into Linux, in my Junior year of High School in 1999. After joining the Navy in 2000, I didn't touch Linux again until 2009 when I was introduced to Ubuntu. Unfortunately, Linux still wasn't ready for gaming, so I dropped it again after a couple months. Then 2019 came around and I began playing with it again after STEAM began talking about SteamOS, but this was still just for funzies as I was primarily using Win10.

In 2020 I decided to start playing with Linux more seriously since I had so much more time on my hands, but it was still secondary to Win10. When Microsoft launched Win11, I quickly made up my mind that I was keeping with Win10, until MS said they were abandoning it and forcing people onto Win11. At this point, I began making serious strides to become Linux-only with my new PC build. As of Dec2024, I am 100% Linux based on my gaming desktop AND my Framework Laptop, and I couldn't be happier.

Primary OS shifts between Bazzite and CachyOS, and I can still play every game I own.

Author: @GamersNexus
Content:
This event was super fun! Not everything in here is because of Windows 10 support ending; Kramden does this all the time, for any computer or reason. That's also why you see some Macs in here. Some more background if you're curious: Kramden gets a mix of e-waste and donated / retired machines from local individuals and from companies. Sometimes, these have perfectly good hardware, sometimes they have one or two broken things. They then work with volunteers (like in this episode) to reclaim anything valuable that could be used for education or cobbled-together into a new machine. A good example is the 12700K: This was in there because some company or person got rid of the computer, but obviously that's still a great part. The next step is to identify whatever was broken in the system, save the good parts, and repurpose them (or sell them to fund the classroom program). Anything unusable, such as just broken hardware or obsolete hardware, is broken down into recyclables and trash, sorted, and sent to the right groups to smelt down or dispose of. They are awesome.
Find Kramden here! https://kramden.org/ (they do local sales also of donated items, sometimes including things we drop off! They also do classes and training on how to use computers, including Ubuntu)
Find Canonical and Ubuntu here: https://ubuntu.com/
